title: The Lost Compass
summary: A boy on a desert camping trip loses his compass and must find his way back to camp before dark using landmarks and the stars.
poll: If you get lost, the smartest thing to do is keep walking in any direction.

versions.title: The Lost Compass
versions.text:
Fahad is camping with his dad in the desert. Dad has a compass. He shows Fahad how to use it to find directions.

In the day, Fahad sees a small fox. He runs after it over a big dune. He goes far from camp.

The sun sinks low near the horizon. Fahad reaches for his compass. It is gone! He is lost, and his heart beats fast.

Fahad stops. He takes a deep breath. He stays calm. Dad said: look for landmarks you know.

Fahad sees a big red rock. He saw this landmark before. He walks that way. He also sees an old tree.

The sky gets dark. A bright star comes out. Dad said this star points north. Camp is north of the rock.

Fahad walks on and sees smoke. It is the camp fire! Dad gives him a big hug. Fahad stayed calm, and he found his way home.

versions.title: The Lost Compass
versions.text:
Fahad is camping with his father in the desert. It is their first full weekend trip. His father gave him a small compass. He showed Fahad how to use it to find directions.

One afternoon, Fahad sees a small fox near some rocks. He runs after it. He climbs over a tall sand dune. He goes much farther from camp than he planned.

The sun begins to sink toward the horizon. Fahad checks his pocket for the compass. It is gone! He is lost, and his heart beats very fast.

Fahad stops. He takes a slow, deep breath. He tries to stay calm. He remembers his father's words: look for landmarks you already know.

Fahad looks around. He sees a tall red rock. He remembers passing it before. He walks toward it. He also spots an old, dry tree he saw earlier.

The sky grows dark. A bright star appears. His father once said this star always points north. Their camp sits just north of the red rock.

Fahad walks on. At last he sees smoke rising in the distance. It is the camp fire! His father gives him a big hug. By staying calm, Fahad found his way home.

One quiet afternoon, Fahad sees a small fennec fox darting near some rocks. He runs after it right away. He climbs over a tall sand dune. He goes much farther from camp than he had planned.

The sun slowly starts to sink toward the horizon. Fahad checks his pocket for the compass. It is gone! A wave of fear rushes through him. He knows he is lost, and his heart begins to pound.

Fahad stops walking. He takes a slow, deep breath. He works hard to stay calm, just as his father once showed him. He remembers what his father once said: look for landmarks you already know.

Fahad looks carefully at the horizon. He sees a tall red rock. He is sure he passed it before. He walks toward it. Soon he sees an old, twisted tree too.

The sky slowly grows dark. One bright star appears above the horizon. His father once said this star always points north. Their camp lies just north of the rock.

Fahad walks on with new hope. At last he sees thin smoke curling in the sky. It is the camp fire! His father runs to hug him, proud that Fahad stayed calm and found his way home.

By the time Fahad stops to look around, the sun is sinking toward the horizon, and the silhouette of distant hills has turned a deep orange-red. He checks his pocket for the compass, but it is gone. A rush of panic sweeps through him, and his heart begins pounding loudly in his chest.

Fahad forces himself to stop moving. He takes a slow, steady breath. He works hard to push the panic away, just as his father once taught him. He remembers his father's advice: stop, breathe, and look for landmarks you already know, then retrace your steps.

Scanning the horizon, Fahad spots a tall red rock that he is almost sure he passed earlier that day. He walks steadily toward it, retracing his path. Soon he notices a dry, twisted old tree standing nearby, another landmark from his walk.

As the sky slowly darkens, one bright star appears low above the horizon. His father once explained that sailors and desert travelers use that star to find direction at night, because it always points north. Their camp lies just north of the red rock.

Walking on with new confidence, Fahad finally spots a thin trail of smoke curling into the darkening sky. It is the camp fire at last! His father runs to meet him with a relieved hug, proud that his son stayed calm and used both landmarks and stars to find his way home.

keyWords.definition: a tool with a needle that always points north, used to find directions
keyWords.example: Hadi used a compass to find his way through the forest.

keyWords.definition: something you can see and remember, like a rock or tree, that helps you find your way
keyWords.example: The old clock tower is a landmark near my school.

keyWords.definition: the line far away where the land seems to meet the sky
keyWords.example: We watched the sun rise over the horizon.

keyWords.definition: a hill of sand made by the wind
keyWords.example: The children raced each other down the tall dune.

keyWords.definition: quiet and not worried or upset
keyWords.example: She stayed calm when she could not find her shoes.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who loses his compass and finds his way back to camp
A boy who buys a new pet fox from a desert market in town
A family that decides to move to a new desert town far from the sea
A boy who learns how to cook food over a campfire with his uncle
questions.why: The whole story follows Fahad after he loses his compass and must find his way back to camp.

wrong.B: The story is not about buying a pet fox.
wrong.C: The family is only camping, not moving.
wrong.D: Cooking is not part of the story.

questions.stem: What does Fahad lose while chasing the fox?
options: his shoe
his compass
his hat
his water bottle
questions.why: In the story, Fahad reaches for his compass, but it is gone.

wrong.A: The story never mentions a shoe.
wrong.C: The story never mentions a hat.
wrong.D: The story never mentions a water bottle.

questions.stem: What animal does Fahad chase?
options: a lizard
a camel
a fennec fox
a bird
questions.why: In the story, Fahad sees a small fennec fox and runs after it.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a lizard.
wrong.B: The story does not mention a camel.
wrong.D: The story does not mention a bird.

questions.stem: In the story, a landmark is —
options: a hill of sand in the desert that people climb
a bright star in the night sky that sailors follow
something you remember to help you find your way
a tool with a needle, used to sew cloth and tents
questions.why: Fahad uses the red rock and the old tree as landmarks, things he remembers to help find his way.

wrong.A: A hill of sand is a dune, not a landmark.
wrong.B: A star is not called a landmark in the story.
wrong.D: A tool with a needle is the compass.

questions.stem: Why does Fahad stop and take a deep breath?
options: He is thirsty
He wants to stay calm and think
He is tired from running
He wants to rest before sleeping
questions.why: Fahad is scared after getting lost, so he breathes to stay calm and think clearly.

wrong.A: The story does not say he is thirsty.
wrong.C: He stops to think, not just to rest from running.
wrong.D: It is not yet time to sleep.

questions.stem: Why does Fahad chase the fox in the first place?
options: He is curious and wants to see where it goes
He wants to catch it for dinner at the camp
His father told him to chase it away
He is trying to find the old camp
questions.why: Fahad runs after the fox without thinking, which shows he is just curious and having fun.

wrong.B: The story never says Fahad wants to eat the fox.
wrong.C: His father is resting, not telling him to chase it.
wrong.D: Chasing the fox is what makes him lost, not how he finds the camp.

questions.stem: How does the bright star help Fahad?
options: It lights up the whole desert
It scares the fox away
It shows him which way is north
It tells him what time it is
questions.why: Fahad's father told him that star always points north, so it helps him know which way to walk.

wrong.A: One star does not light up the whole desert.
wrong.B: The star does not scare the fox; the fox is already gone.
wrong.D: The star shows direction, not time.

questions.stem: What happens right before Fahad sees the smoke from the campfire?
options: He finds the tall red rock along his path to the hills
He loses his compass somewhere on the trail behind him
He chases the small fox near the camp at dusk
He watches the star appear and checks his direction
questions.why: Fahad uses the star to check his direction, and only after that does he spot the smoke and reach camp.

wrong.A: He finds the red rock earlier, before the star appears.
wrong.B: Losing the compass happens near the start of the story.
wrong.C: Chasing the fox happens near the start of the story.

LOW.prompt: Imagine you were lost like Fahad. Write about what you would do to stay calm and find your way back. Use at least two ideas from the story.
checklist: I explained what I would do to stay calm.
I used at least two ideas from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: If I were lost like Fahad, I would stop and take a deep breath so I could stay calm. Then I would look for a landmark I remembered, like a big rock or an old tree. I would also watch for a bright star, because it can show which way is north. Staying calm would help me think clearly and find my way back.

keyWords.definition: to find your way from one place to another
keyWords.example: Sailors use the stars to navigate across the sea.

keyWords.definition: the way something points or the way you need to go
keyWords.example: The signpost showed the direction to the village.

keyWords.definition: a sudden strong feeling of fear that makes it hard to think
keyWords.example: He felt panic rise when the lights suddenly went out.

keyWords.definition: to go back over a path you already walked
keyWords.example: We had to retrace our steps to find the lost key.

keyWords.definition: the dark outline or shape of something seen against the light
keyWords.example: We could see the silhouette of the mountain against the evening sky.

questions.stem: Which sentence best tells what this story is mainly about?
options: A boy learns that staying calm and using landmarks and stars helps him when he is lost
A boy decides he will never go camping again with his father in the desert
A fennec fox leads a boy safely back to his family's camp every single night
A father buys his son a brand new compass as a surprise birthday gift
questions.why: The story follows Fahad as he gets lost and uses calm thinking, landmarks, and the stars to find his way home.

wrong.B: The story never says Fahad refuses to camp again.
wrong.C: The fox does not lead Fahad back; he finds his own way.
wrong.D: The compass was already Fahad's grandfather's, and it is lost, not given as a new gift.

questions.stem: Whose compass did Fahad's father give him?
options: a compass his father bought at a store
a compass that belonged to Fahad's grandfather
a compass borrowed from a kind neighbor down the street
a compass found abandoned somewhere in the desert sand
questions.why: In the story, the compass once belonged to Fahad's grandfather.

wrong.A: The story does not say it was bought at a store.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a neighbor.
wrong.D: The story does not say it was found in the desert.

questions.stem: What did Fahad's father teach him to use?
options: A map
A phone
A compass
A flashlight
questions.why: In the story, his father taught Fahad how to find his way with a compass.

wrong.A: A map is not what his father taught him to use.
wrong.B: A phone is not what he learned to use.
wrong.D: A flashlight does not show direction.

questions.stem: In the story, the word silhouette refers to —
options: the bright, warm light of the midday sun
the whistling sound of the desert wind
a small, furry kind of desert animal
the dark outline of the hills against the sky
questions.why: The story describes the silhouette of distant hills turning orange-red against the fading light.

wrong.A: A silhouette is a dark shape, not bright light.
wrong.B: A silhouette is something seen, not heard.
wrong.C: A silhouette is not an animal; it is a shape.

questions.stem: Why does panic rush through Fahad when he realizes his compass is gone?
options: He is cold and shivering in the evening air
He is suddenly unsure how to find his way back
He is angry at the fox for running away
He is hungry and wants his dinner soon
questions.why: Without the compass, Fahad no longer has an easy way to check direction, so fear rushes through him.

wrong.A: The story does not mention cold or shivering.
wrong.C: The story does not say Fahad is angry at the fox.
wrong.D: The story does not mention hunger.

questions.stem: Compare how Fahad feels right after losing the compass with how he feels after remembering his father's advice.
options: He feels panicked at first, then calmer after he focuses on his father's advice
He feels perfectly calm the whole time and never worries at all, even when lost
He feels angry at first, and then feels quite sad later on in the evening
He feels tired at first, and then feels very excited later on after supper
questions.why: Fahad first feels a rush of panic, but after stopping to breathe and remember his father's advice, he moves forward with steady confidence.

wrong.B: The story clearly describes panic, not constant calm.
wrong.C: The story never describes anger or sadness.
wrong.D: The story never describes tiredness or excitement about being lost.

questions.stem: Why does the bright star in the sky help Fahad find north?
options: It is the brightest light in the whole desert
It moves closer to camp as the night goes on
It always points toward the north, as his father explained
It makes the red rock much easier to see at night time
questions.why: In the story, his father told him the star always points toward the north.

wrong.A: The story does not compare it to every other light in the desert.
wrong.B: Stars do not move closer; they appear in a fixed direction.
wrong.D: The star helps with direction, not with seeing the rock.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order: Fahad spots the red rock; Fahad's compass goes missing; Fahad sees the star and checks direction; Fahad reaches the campfire.
options: compass missing, rock, star, campfire
campfire, star, compass missing, rock
star, rock, compass missing, campfire
compass missing, star, rock, campfire
questions.why: Fahad first loses the compass, then spots the red rock while retracing his steps, then checks his direction using the star, and finally reaches the campfire.

wrong.B: This reverses the order completely.
wrong.C: The compass must go missing before Fahad starts looking for landmarks.
wrong.D: Fahad spots the rock before he uses the star, not after.

MID.prompt: Explain how Fahad used both calm thinking and knowledge of landmarks and stars to find his way back to camp. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Fahad stayed calm.
I explained how he used landmarks and the stars.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: When Fahad realized his compass was missing, panic rushed through him, but he stopped and took a slow breath to calm down. He then looked for landmarks he recognized, like the red rock and the old tree, and retraced his steps toward them. As it grew dark, he used the bright star that always points north to check his direction. By staying calm and using both landmarks and the star, Fahad found his way safely back to the campfire.

keyWords.definition: to figure out your direction or position compared to your surroundings
keyWords.example: Hikers often use a map to orient themselves in unfamiliar terrain.

keyWords.definition: a group of stars that forms a pattern in the night sky
keyWords.example: Ancient sailors named constellations after animals and heroes.

keyWords.definition: confused about which direction you are facing or where you are
keyWords.example: She felt disoriented after stepping off the spinning ride.

keyWords.definition: good at finding quick and clever ways to solve problems
keyWords.example: The resourceful campers used branches to build a shelter in the rain.

keyWords.definition: a natural feeling or reaction that happens without thinking it through
keyWords.example: Her instinct told her to pull her hand away from the hot pan.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this story?
options: Fahad decides that camping in the desert is too dangerous for him to try again
A disoriented boy finds his way home by staying calm and reading landmarks and stars
A fennec fox becomes lost in the desert and must be rescued by Fahad
A father teaches his son how to build a campfire using dry branches
questions.why: The story centers on Fahad becoming disoriented and then calmly using landmarks and the stars to make his way back.

wrong.A: The story ends with a relieved hug, not a decision to quit camping.
wrong.C: The fox is never lost; Fahad is the one who gets lost.
wrong.D: The story focuses on navigation, not campfire building.

questions.stem: In the story, disoriented most nearly means —
options: confused about direction or location
excited and eager to start the trip today
angry and upset about the long and lost day
exhausted from walking all day in the hot sun
questions.why: Fahad becomes disoriented after losing his compass, meaning he no longer knows which way to go.

wrong.B: Being disoriented is not the same as being excited.
wrong.C: The story describes fear and panic, not anger.
wrong.D: Disoriented describes confusion, not tiredness.

questions.stem: What detail about Fahad's compass connects him to his family's past?
options: It was a gift from a stranger
It was bought the morning of the trip
It once belonged to his grandfather
It was found along the trail
questions.why: The story notes that the compass had once belonged to Fahad's grandfather.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a stranger giving the compass.
wrong.B: The story does not say it was bought that morning.
wrong.D: The story does not say it was found along the trail.

questions.stem: What in the story suggests that chasing the fox was an instinctive reaction rather than a planned decision?
options: Fahad carefully studied a detailed map before he ever moved
Fahad asked his father for permission before running
Fahad had carefully planned the chase the night before
The story says he chased it 'instinctively,' without thinking twice
questions.why: The text specifically describes Fahad chasing the fox instinctively and without thinking twice, showing it was unplanned.

wrong.A: The story never mentions Fahad studying a map beforehand.
wrong.B: The story never mentions him asking permission.
wrong.C: The story gives no indication the chase was planned in advance.

questions.stem: Compare Fahad's state of mind right after losing the compass with his state of mind once he begins following his father's method.
options: He moves from disoriented panic to focused, steady action
He remains equally fearful throughout both moments
He feels proud at first, then ashamed later
He feels bored at first, then alarmed later
questions.why: Fahad first feels disoriented panic, but once he applies his father's method of stopping, breathing, and finding landmarks, he becomes steady and confident.

wrong.B: His fear clearly lessens once he follows the method.
wrong.C: The story never describes pride turning to shame.
wrong.D: The story never describes boredom at the start.

questions.stem: Why have sailors and desert travelers relied on that particular star for centuries?
options: It is part of a constellation that only appears once a year
It always points toward the north, regardless of season or location
It is the only star visible in the desert sky
It changes color to warn of storms
questions.why: The story explains that the star always points toward the north no matter the season or location, making it a reliable guide.

wrong.A: The story does not say it appears only once a year.
wrong.C: The story describes a full constellation, not a single visible star.
wrong.D: The story never mentions the star changing color.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly matches the method Fahad uses to find his way home?
options: Reach the camp, confirm direction with the star, retrace steps using landmarks, stop and breathe
Retrace steps using landmarks, reach the camp, stop and breathe, confirm direction with the star
Stop and breathe, retrace steps using landmarks, confirm direction with the star, reach the camp
Confirm direction with the star, stop and breathe, reach the camp, retrace steps using landmarks
questions.why: Fahad first stops and breathes to calm down, then retraces his steps using landmarks, then confirms his direction with the star, and finally reaches camp.

wrong.A: This places reaching camp before the steps that lead there.
wrong.B: This places reaching camp before Fahad even calms down.
wrong.D: This places confirming direction before Fahad has calmed down.

questions.stem: Why does the author most likely include the detail that the compass once belonged to Fahad's grandfather?
options: To explain why the compass was old and easily broken when it fell in the sand
To suggest that Fahad's grandfather was lost in the same desert many years before
To explain why Fahad was not resourceful and had never travelled before
To add a sense of family history and show why the compass mattered to Fahad
questions.why: Mentioning the grandfather's compass gives the object personal and family significance beyond its practical use.

wrong.A: The story never says the compass was fragile.
wrong.B: The story never mentions the grandfather getting lost.
wrong.C: Fahad's actions show he is resourceful, not the opposite.

HIGH.prompt: The story shows that staying calm can be just as important as having the right tools. Do you agree or disagree? Support your answer with evidence from the story about Fahad's experience.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed a point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that staying calm can be just as important as having the right tools. Even though Fahad lost his compass, he was able to find his way home because he stopped to breathe and think instead of panicking. His resourcefulness in using the red rock, the old tree, and the star shows that knowledge and a calm mind matter more than any single tool. Someone might argue that the compass was essential and that Fahad was simply lucky to remember the landmarks, but his father had trained that instinct in him specifically so he would be ready, which shows that calm thinking is a skill, not luck.

LOW.stem: What does Fahad see after he sees the big red rock?
options: A small fox
An old tree
A tall tent
A deep lake
LOW.why: The text says he also sees an old tree after the red rock.

wrong.A: The fox was seen earlier, in the day.
wrong.C: The text does not say he sees a tent first.
wrong.D: No lake is in the story.

LOW.stem: Why does Fahad's heart beat fast?
options: He ran a long race
He hears a loud sound
He is lost
He is very hungry
LOW.why: In the story, he knows he is lost, and his heart beats fast.

wrong.A: He chased a fox earlier, but the text links his fast heart to being lost.
wrong.B: The text does not mention a loud sound.
wrong.D: Hunger is not mentioned in the story.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word horizon means the place where —
options: the sky seems to meet the land
a little fox hides in a deep hole
Dad keeps his compass at night
a camp fire is lit for the night
LOW.why: The sun sinks low near the horizon, which is where the sky seems to meet the land.

wrong.B: The story does not use horizon for a fox hole.
wrong.C: Dad's compass is not kept at the horizon.
wrong.D: The camp fire is on the ground at the camp.

LOW.stem: How does Dad most likely feel when Fahad comes back?
options: Angry and cold
Sleepy and bored
Glad he is safe
Afraid of the dark
LOW.why: Dad gives Fahad a big hug, which shows he is glad Fahad is safe.

wrong.A: A big hug does not show anger.
wrong.B: A hug does not show boredom.
wrong.D: The text does not say Dad is afraid.

MID.stem: What is Fahad's father doing when Fahad sees the fox?
options: Cooking dinner
Resting near the tent
Looking for the compass
Walking over a dune
MID.why: The story says his father rests near the tent.

wrong.A: Cooking is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The compass is lost later, and Fahad is the one who looks for it.
wrong.D: Fahad is the one who goes over the dune.

MID.stem: What does "Without thinking" show about Fahad's choice to chase the fox?
options: He made a careful plan
He asked his father first
He did it only at night
He acted fast, with no plan
MID.why: The words show Fahad ran after the fox right away and did not stop to plan.

wrong.A: Acting without thinking is the opposite of planning.
wrong.B: His father was resting and was not asked.
wrong.C: The chase happens on a quiet afternoon.

MID.stem: In the story, the word retrace means to —
options: walk back along the same path
draw a map of the whole desert
ask a stranger for some help
climb up a very tall tree
MID.why: Fahad walks toward the rock "retracing his path," which means going back along the way he came.

wrong.B: Fahad does not draw a map.
wrong.C: No stranger appears in the story.
wrong.D: Fahad does not climb a tree.

MID.stem: Why is Fahad's father proud of him at the end?
options: Fahad caught the little fox in the dunes
Fahad stayed calm and found his way
Fahad built a camp fire all by himself
Fahad found the lost compass in the sand
MID.why: The story says his father is proud that Fahad stayed calm and used landmarks and stars to get home.

wrong.A: The fox is not the reason for his pride.
wrong.C: His father's camp fire is what Fahad finds.
wrong.D: The compass is never found.

HIGH.stem: About how far beyond his plan did Fahad wander from camp?
options: Nearly two kilometers
Only a few steps
Nearly twenty kilometers
About two hundred meters
HIGH.why: The story says he wandered nearly two kilometers farther from camp than he had meant to.

wrong.B: A few steps would not leave him lost.
wrong.C: Twenty kilometers is far too large.
wrong.D: Two hundred meters is too small.

HIGH.stem: How did Fahad lose his compass?
options: A fox snatched it out of his hand
He left it behind in the tent that morning
It slipped out of his pocket along the path
His father took it back without telling him
HIGH.why: The story says it must have slipped out somewhere along the path without his noticing.

wrong.A: The fox only darted between rocks.
wrong.B: He reached into his pocket, so he had carried it.
wrong.D: His father is resting at camp.

HIGH.stem: In the last paragraph, the word resourceful describes someone who is —
options: very tired and rather slow
good at solving problems
afraid of the dark night
very fond of small animals
HIGH.why: Fahad stayed calm and used landmarks and stars to find his way, which shows he can solve problems.

wrong.A: Nothing in the story says he is slow.
wrong.C: He faced the dark calmly.
wrong.D: His chasing the fox does not describe this word.

HIGH.stem: Why does Fahad stop moving and take a slow breath when he realizes he is lost?
options: To calm down and use his training
To wake up his sleeping father at camp
To scare away the little fennec fox
To check the needle of his compass
HIGH.why: He is trusting the instinct his father trained into him to push away panic.

wrong.B: His father is far away at camp.
wrong.C: The fox is gone by then.
wrong.D: The compass is already lost.
